wine.name: Catena Zapata Adrianna Vineyard River Stones Malbec
wine.grapes: Malbec, from the family's own selection of old vines taken from its Angélica vineyard in Lunlunta.
wine.sites: River Stones, a small parcel of the Adrianna Vineyard in Gualtallary, Tupungato, at about 1,370 metres by the house's sheets, on the bed of an ancient river whose stones are coated white with calcium carbonate.
wine.making: Cold soaked for some days, then fermented over two to three weeks, with part of the vat in whole bunches in some later vintages. Élevage runs well over a year in French oak, in barrels in the early vintages and in large, old foudres in later ones; the months and the vessels change with the vintage.
wine.glass: Violet and blackberry over black cherry, with a stony, faintly metallic edge, fresh acidity and long, smooth tannin; taut and lifted rather than plush.
wine.ageing: It opens slowly in bottle after a tight first five years or so, and has the acidity and tannin to keep for well over a decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The family's vineyard in Gualtallary, planted in 1992 and named for the youngest daughter of the founder's grandson.
The parcel's name, for the old riverbed of white stones it grows on; recent labels shorten it to River.

records.table: High in Gualtallary, one parcel of Catena Zapata's Adrianna Vineyard lies on an old riverbed whose stones are coated white with calcium carbonate, and its Malbec is bottled as River Stones. Taut rather than plush, with a violet scent, it repays a few years in bottle and a decanter.
records.story: Italian by birth, the Catena family's founder reached Argentina in 1898 and planted his first Malbec vineyard in Mendoza in 1902, by the family's own account; the house counts four generations since. His son, in the family's telling, held that Malbec could stand beside the wines of France, and his grandson, back from a visiting professorship at the University of California, Berkeley, in the early 1980s, turned the house towards fine wine, first with Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay and then with Malbec. In 1992 the family planted the Adrianna Vineyard at about 1,450 metres in Gualtallary, in the Tupungato department of the Uco Valley, and named it for the grandson's youngest daughter. Its Malbec came from the family's own selection, taken from Lot 18 of its old Angélica vineyard in Lunlunta, Maipú. The new vineyard was divided into parcels and studied closely, and the Catena Institute of Wine has published research from it. River Stones is the parcel on the bed of an ancient river, its stones coated white with calcium carbonate, bottled apart from its neighbours Fortuna Terrae and Mundus Bacillus Terrae. Recent labels shorten its name to Adrianna Vineyard River. Set beside a Luján de Cuyo Malbec, it shows how far altitude and stone have carried the grape from that plush style.

wine.name: Achaval-Ferrer Finca Altamira Malbec
wine.grapes: Old vine Malbec, with no other grape.
wine.sites: Finca Altamira, an old Malbec vineyard in La Consulta, within Paraje Altamira in the San Carlos department, at about 1,050 to 1,100 metres on alluvial ground with a shallow surface of silt, sand and volcanic ash.
wine.making: Cement vats hold the ferment, worked by open pump overs; by the house's own sheet there is no cold soak, no added enzyme and no correction of acidity. The wine then ages for a little over a year in French oak barrels, most of them new, and goes into bottle without filtration.
wine.glass: Black cherry, blackberry and violet, with graphite and wet slate beneath; vigorous acidity and fine, chalky tannin give it tension and grip rather than sweetness.
wine.ageing: After a firm, closed youth it needs five years or more, and a strong vintage keeps well beyond a decade.
wine.serve: Pour at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius into a large Bordeaux glass, a young bottle after an hour or two in a decanter.

label.means: The named old vineyard in La Consulta; finca means farm or estate and carries no legal rank.
Only the province is named, though the grapes all grow in one Uco Valley vineyard.

records.table: From the vintage of 1999, Finca Altamira was the first wine Achaval-Ferrer released: Malbec from one old vineyard in La Consulta, in the Uco Valley. Expect violet, black cherry and a chalky grip; decant it and pour it beside red meat.
records.story: By its own story, Achaval-Ferrer began with a group of Argentine and Italian friends who travelled thousands of kilometres in search of old vineyards before they came upon Finca Altamira in 1998. Its old Malbec vines in La Consulta, in the south of the Uco Valley, gave the house its founding idea: to bottle each old vineyard on its own rather than blend Mendoza into one wine. Finca Altamira 1999 was the first wine the house released, made from very low yields. Single vineyard Malbecs from Finca Bella Vista in Luján de Cuyo and Finca Mirador in Medrano followed beside it, with Quimera as the blend across sites. In 2011 the SPI group, owner of the Stolichnaya vodka brand, bought into the house. In 2013 Paraje Altamira, the alluvial fan of the Tunuyán river around the vineyard, became one of Argentina's geographical indications, its boundary drawn by soil survey: official recognition of the case for site that single vineyard bottlings such as this one had made. Finca Altamira teaches Mendoza Malbec by place, its chalky grip coming from the ground rather than from the cellar.

wine.name: Zuccardi Finca Piedra Infinita
wine.grapes: Malbec alone, drawn from several plots of the one vineyard.
wine.sites: The Piedra Infinita vineyard at about 1,100 metres in Paraje Altamira, on the alluvial fan of the Tunuyán river: a sandy surface over granite stones and boulders coated in calcium carbonate.
wine.making: Its ferment runs in concrete vats without an epoxy lining, on the grapes' own yeasts. The early vintages were aged partly in used 500 litre French oak barrels and partly in concrete; the house's sheets of 2019 and 2022 give concrete alone for the ageing, with no oak at all.
wine.glass: Wet stone and dried herbs under violet and black pepper, with a chalky, finely grained grip and fresh acidity; grain and tension count for more in it than ripe sweetness.
wine.ageing: Stony and reserved on release, it gains depth over its first decade, and its acidity carries it beyond.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius, a little cooler than a plush Malbec, in a large Bordeaux glass; a young bottle takes an hour of decanting.

label.means: The geographical indication of the Tunuyán river's alluvial fan in San Carlos, recognised in 2013 and drawn by soil.
The vineyard's name, infinite stone in Spanish, for the stones that fill its ground.

records.table: Granite stones fill the Paraje Altamira vineyard behind Familia Zuccardi's Finca Piedra Infinita, a Malbec fermented and aged in concrete rather than new oak. Pour it a little cool: violet, pepper and wet stone sit over a chalky grip.
records.story: The house dates itself to 1963, when its founder, an engineer, planted the family's first vineyard in Mendoza to show off an irrigation system he had devised; the vineyard drew the family into wine. In 2007 it planted its first vineyard in the Uco Valley, Finca Canal Uco in Paraje Altamira, and then the Piedra Infinita and Los Membrillos vineyards nearby. Piedra Infinita lies on the alluvial fan of the Tunuyán river, where granite stones and boulders coated in calcium carbonate lie under a sandy surface. Paraje Altamira was recognised as a geographical indication in 2013, the year building began on the Zuccardi Valle de Uco winery. It opened in 2016, raised in part from the stones of the Piedra Infinita vineyard itself. The wine named for that vineyard is fermented there in concrete with native yeasts; its early vintages also saw used 500 litre barrels, and the house's sheets of 2019 and 2022 have it aged in concrete alone. Single plots of the same vineyard, such as Gravascal, are bottled beside it, and so is Concreto, which puts the vessel on its label. In this wine Mendoza Malbec turns away from ripeness and new oak, towards stone, freshness and a named place.

wine.name: Cheval des Andes
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec, their proportions changing markedly with the vintage, with a little Petit Verdot in some years.
wine.sites: Old Malbec at Las Compuertas in Luján de Cuyo, ungrafted and partly planted in 1929, long watered by flooding from snowmelt channels, with higher fruit from the house's vineyard in Paraje Altamira in the Uco Valley.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented parcel by parcel in small vats of 30 to 80 hectolitres. After the malolactic fermentation the teams of Cheval des Andes and Château Cheval Blanc build the first blend together, and the wine then ages for thirteen to eighteen months, by vintage, in barrels and larger casks, new and used, mostly of French oak.
wine.glass: Cedar and tobacco beneath blackberry, cassis and violet, with polished, fine grained tannin and a fresh, long finish; it reads more like Bordeaux than like plush Mendoza.
wine.ageing: Polished enough to drink within a few years of release, it has the structure to develop over fifteen years or more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a young bottle goes into a decanter an hour or so ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: French for horse of the Andes, after Château Cheval Blanc, the Bordeaux partner in the wine.
Origin at the level of the province, the grapes drawn from Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley.

records.table: Château Cheval Blanc and Terrazas de los Andes make Cheval des Andes together in Mendoza, blending Cabernet Sauvignon with old, ungrafted Malbec from Las Compuertas. Cedar and violet come before plush fruit; serve it as you would a red Bordeaux.
records.story: The Malbec at Las Compuertas, in Luján de Cuyo, was planted in 1929 and long watered in the old way, by flooding from the snowmelt channels whose floodgates give the place its name. Flooding drowns phylloxera, so the vines could grow on their own roots, as Bordeaux's vines did before the louse reached France in the nineteenth century. As the house tells it, the head of Château Cheval Blanc saw in these vines a road back to the Bordeaux of that time, and in 1999 the Saint-Émilion estate joined Terrazas de los Andes, the Mendoza house founded by Moët Hennessy in 1996, to make one wine. The first vintage was 1999. Each parcel is fermented apart, and after the malolactic fermentation the teams of both houses meet to build the first blend, as a Bordeaux château assembles its grand vin from many lots. Higher fruit from the house's vineyard in Paraje Altamira, in the Uco Valley, joins the old vines. For a sommelier, Cheval des Andes is Argentina's place in the set of French joint ventures abroad, beside Opus One in Napa and Almaviva in Chile, and a lesson in Malbec given a Bordeaux frame.

table, traps[0] and questions[0]: Cabernet Sauvignon is named first and Malbec is no longer said to lead.
open: The founding: 1999 in the library and most accounts, with the first vintage of 1999; Wine Folly's guide says established in 1998.
Drip irrigation came in 2017 by the house's Savoir-Faire page and in 2018 by Lay and Wheeler; the record dates neither and says only that the vines were long flooded.
Terrazas de los Andes founded by Moët Hennessy in 1996 rests on Wikipedia and one guide page; no primary was found.

wine.name: Norton Privada
wine.grapes: Malbec in the lead, with Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, in a blend that shifts with the vintage.
wine.sites: Old vines, fifty to ninety years old by the house's own sheet, from its vineyards at La Colonia, Lunlunta and Agrelo.
wine.making: Three days of cold soak come before a ferment of about ten days. A year to sixteen months in French oak barrels follows, by vintage, then six months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Dark plum, blackberry and kirsch over cassis and dark chocolate, with a touch of cola and toasty barrel; full, ripe and supple, in the plush style of Luján de Cuyo.
wine.ageing: Ready within a few years of the vintage, it keeps for ten years and more by the house's own reckoning.
wine.serve: A Bordeaux glass at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, the bottle decanted an hour ahead when young.

records.table: Bodega Norton, the Luján de Cuyo house of 1895, calls its old vine blend Privada, private: Malbec with Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, aged in French oak. Plum, kirsch and dark chocolate make it a ripe, supple partner for grilled beef.
records.story: Edmund James Palmer Norton (1865 to 1944), an English engineer, came to Argentina to help build the railway across the Andes and settled in Mendoza. In 1895 he founded his own house at Perdriel in Luján de Cuyo, planting vines brought from France in what the house calls the first vineyard south of the Mendoza river. The house kept his name, and in 1989 it was bought by a member of the Austrian Swarovski crystal family. In 1997 it bought Finca La Colonia, and by its own account it was among the first four wineries to take the controlled appellation of Luján de Cuyo. Privada, the house says, began as a request from the Swarovski family to the house's winemaker: a wine to drink among intimates and to welcome friends, and the Spanish name, private, says so. It blends Malbec with Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon from vines of fifty to ninety years, aged in French oak. Norton Privada is the classic Luján de Cuyo blend: Malbec in the lead, two Bordeaux grapes beside it and the plush frame of the province's historic first zone, from a house whose story runs back to the railway age.

report: Not in the library: the founding of 1895, the railway, the vines from France and the purchase of 1989 rest on the house's own history page with Wikipedia and the Wein-Plus glossary as second sources.

The founder's dates, 1865 to 1944, rest on Wikipedia and the Wein-Plus glossary; both call him Sir, a title no other source read confirms, so the record does not; one account dates the founding to 1885 against 1895 everywhere else.
Privada's first vintage was not found (Wine.com lists vintages back to 2006, and a later source speaks of critics following it since 2002), so the record gives no year.

The blend shifts: 40 per cent Malbec with 30 each of Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon on the house's sheet and in 2014, and 60, 20 and 20 in 2023 on Wine.com; the making joins the house's sheet (three day cold soak, ten day fermentation, sixteen months in French oak, six in bottle) with Wine.com's 2014 and 2009 notes (cement vats, about twelve months in new and second use oak; native yeasts, sixteen months new oak).
Recent releases are sold by the house as Privada Family Blend; the record keeps the plan's Norton Privada, and a rename that keeps the key may be weighed.

The house's top blend is named for its buyer of 1989; it is left out of others, as whether he is living was not settled, and the buyer's son, who bought Finca La Colonia in 1997, is living and unnamed.

The pick stands, though Privada is the house's classic blend rather than its highest tier; the first vineyard south of the Mendoza river is the house's claim, with Wikipedia's first winery south of the river as a second account, and the first four DOC wineries the house's alone, both hedged.

changed: wine.appellation and wine.label: Mendoza became Luján de Cuyo, the appellation the house's own Privada Family Blend page gives and wine-searcher lists; the label line now says what that zone is.

wine.making: the cement vats and the new and used barrels rested on one merchant's notes of 2014 and are cut; the oak time is a year to sixteen months by vintage, on the house's sheet, that merchant and a Portuguese merchant's sixteen months in French oak.
others[0].note: the claim of being among the first four D.O.C. wineries, the house's alone, is cut from the note; the story keeps it, hedged as the house's account.
traps[1]: the wine's newer name, Privada Family Blend, on the house's page and merchants' listings, is now taught; the plan's name stands.
open: The house places La Colonia, Lunlunta and Agrelo in Luján de Cuyo, while Lunlunta is usually placed in Maipú; the record names the vineyards without placing them.

Among the first four wineries of the D.O.C. rests on the house alone and stays hedged in the story; the lint's note on the first vineyard south of the river is answered by a Spanish travel account and other guides calling it the first winery south of the river.
A Swiss newspaper (Blick) reports the house in court ordered insolvency proceedings; the record tells nothing of the present, but the integrator may weigh the pick.
The founder was born on the border of Prussia and Denmark and raised in England by two accounts; the record keeps an English engineer, as Wikipedia, Wein-Plus and a Spanish account call him.
